title: MB8-26057
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The principal claimant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX; her spouse, XXXX XXXX XXXX; and their children, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, are citizens of Mexico and are claiming refugee protection in Canada pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The principal claimant was named the designated representative of her three minor children pursuant to subsection 167(2) of the IRPA and rule 15 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules.
The panel determines that the claimants are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection" for the following reasons.
Taking all of the evidence into consideration, the panel concludes that the determinative issue is credibility.

The principal claimant's complete allegations are found in the Basis of Claim Form1 (BOC Form), as well as in her written account, attached to her application. The principal claimant's spouse and their three children have adopted these allegations in their own BOC Forms. A brief summary follows.

The claimants fear they will be seriously injured or killed by the principal claimant's former step-mother, XXXX XXXX XXXX, and her partner, XXXX XXXX XXXX, following a dispute regarding the estate of the principal claimant's father and the circumstances of his death. Additionally, they claim that these individuals are members of the Los Cabellaros Templarios cartel.
The principal claimant alleges that her father was burned to death and that her problems started once she began investigating his death.
The claimants left their country for Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018. Identity

The claimants' identities have been established on the grounds of the principal claimants' testimonies as well as on the Mexican passports on the record.2 The panel concludes that their identities and country of reference, Mexico, have been established. ANALYSIS Paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act

The panel verified whether this claim could be analyzed under section 96 of the IRPA. However, none of the Convention grounds of persecution, namely those in section 96 of the IRPA, apply to the present claims.
Therefore, the panel examined this claim under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA. Credibility

The panel took into account the principle that sworn testimony is presumed to be true. However, the panel found significant omissions concerning central factors of the refugee protection claims in the claimants' BOC Forms, which came to light during their testimony at the hearing and could not be reasonably explained. For these reasons, the panel finds that the claimants are not credible.

At the beginning of the hearing, the panel was sure to ask the claimants whether the information found in the BOC Form was complete, true and correct. It also asked whether they wished to add anything else, to which they responded that it was complete. In addition, the panel notes that the original BOC Forms, along with the account, were signed on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, and that the account was amended at the beginning of the hearing in order to correct a date. Death of the principal claimant's father

The panel questioned the female claimant about what she had learned while investigating her father's death. The female claimant answered that her former step-mother, XXXX XXXX confessed to her that she killed her father and made him suffer a great deal. The panel asked the female claimant when she found out about this, to which she responded that she could not remember the exact date but that it was at the end of the lawsuit to settle her father's estate in XXXX 2010. The panel, therefore, invited the female claimant to explain why this information was not included in her BOC Form. She stated that a lot of information had to be edited while writing her account.

The panel does not accept these explanations. Furthermore, the panel is of the opinion that these allegations are crucial elements at the basis of the refugee protection claim and should have been mentioned in her BOC Form. Question 2a) of the female claimant's BOC Form specifically asks to explain in "detail" "[w]hat happened to you and your family." Moreover, the female claimant was represented by an experienced lawyer. The panel is of the view that it is reasonable to expect that information as significant as a confession from XXXX XXXX stating that she killed her father, would be mentioned in her BOC Form.
The panel draws a negative inference about the female claimant's credibility from this significant omission. Threats

The panel questioned the principal claimant about the last time she was threatened, to which she answered that it was in 2016, when individuals went to her son's school and showed a photograph of her to the teacher, asking which child was her son. She also states that it was at this same time, around XXXX 2016, that she was followed by a green Cherokee vehicle that she believes was XXXXandXXXX XXXX. In addition, she states that the last time that she was threatened by telephone was when they lived at XXXX XXXX XXXX. The panel notes that they lived there from XXXX 2016 to XXXX 2017. Then, the panel questioned the female claimant about why she did not mention this telephone threat in her BOC Form. She answered that she had included a lot of information but that her lawyer had cut out certain information.

The panel does not accept these explanations because it does not find them credible. The principal claimant and the other claimants are being represented by an experienced lawyer and the panel does not believe that the lawyer would have cut such significant information from their account.
Therefore, the panel draws a negative inference with regard to her credibility.
The panel notes that between 2007 and 2017, the claimants moved four times to Uruapan, in the state on Michoacan. They claim that they moved by reason of their fear.

As stated in the BOC Form and in her testimony at the hearing, the principal claimant alleges that they moved to Mexico City in XXXX 2017. She testified that they moved to Mexico City with the goal of preparing to leave for Canada and to get all of the necessary documents in order. The panel notes that they lived there for 10 months.

The panel asked her whether she received threats in Mexico City and the principal claimant responded in the negative, but stated that she had changed her telephone number and that she did not answer the telephone when she did not recognize the phone number. However, she did state that XXXXand XXXX paid her sister a visit, asking where she had gone. The female claimant told the panel that she did not tell anyone where she was moving when she left Uruapan; therefore, her sister did not give them any information on this topic. The panel asked the female claimant why she did not mention this in her BOC Form. She answered that there were too many details and that certain details had to be cut out.

The panel is of the opinion that it is reasonable for the female claimant to state in her BOC Form that they continued to search for her because this shows that her agents of persecution have a high level of motivation to find her and harm her.

In light of this significant omission, the panel is of the view that the female claimant attempted to embellish her testimony at the hearing by adding these allegations. Consequently, the panel draws a negative inference as to the principal claimant's credibility.

The panel questioned the claimant XXXX XXXX XXXX about whether he had received threats from XXXXandXXXX XXXX. He answered no, but stated that he did not have a cellphone so that he could not get calls. Furthermore, he stated that when he was in Mexico City, he worked at a little store in his mother's home and did not go out due to his fear. He adds that one day, people came to his mother to ask her whether she knew his wife and where she was, while they were in Mexico City. The panel asked the claimant whether he knew when this happened and he answered that he did not. The panel then asked him why this information had not been documented in his BOC Form. He replied that he did not know, there were so many details in their account.

The panel cannot accept these explanations. As mentioned above, question 2a) of the claimant's BOC Form specifically asks to explain in "detail" "[w]hat happened to you and your family." Moreover, the claimant was represented by an experienced lawyer. At the beginning of the hearing, the panel also asked the claimant whether the information was complete, true and correct. He answered that it was. The panel notes that in his BOC Form, the male claimant answered the questions by referring to the principal claimant's account. As stated earlier, the panel is of the opinion that it is reasonable for the male claimant to mention in his BOC Form that they continued to search for them because this demonstrates that the agents of persecution have a high level of motivation to find them.
The panel draws a negative inference from these responses in relation to the claimant's credibility.

Although all of these omissions on their own would not necessarily be sufficient to undermine the claimants' credibility, when considered as a whole, they seriously undermine the credibility of all of the allegations of pursuits and threats. Documentary evidence submitted by the claimants

Among the items submitted by the principal claimant as evidence was her father's death certificate, along with a newspaper article stating that her father's charred remains had been found. The panel does not doubt that the female claimant's father had died or that he had indeed been killed. However, given the credibility issues raised at the hearing, the panel cannot conclude that the female claimant and her family are at risk and are being sought by XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, and the Los Caballeros Templarios cartel.
The principal claimant also submitted her father and XXXX XXXX XXXX marriage certificate and divorce certificate3 as evidence.

The panel does not doubt that the principal claimant's father had been married to XXXX; however, due to the credibility issues noted at the hearing, the panel cannot conclude that this has any relation to the allegations of fear raised by the principal claimant.

During the hearing, the principal claimant also submitted a letter4 from her lawyer in Mexico, whom she had mandated to obtain documents while she was in Canada, including her father's death certificate and his autopsy report.

The lawyer stated that she had to go to the public prosecutor's office a number of times and that it seemed as though they were hiding information. She added that the last time that she had gone to the office, the person who helped her, followed her to her car and took a picture of her licence plate. She wrote that this caused her fear.

As stated above, the panel gives little weight to this document by reason of the credibility issues raised at the hearing, regarding the allegations that XXXXandXXXX XXXX are searching for the female claimant.

As well, the claimants submitted evidence regarding their change of residence.5 The panel does not doubt that they did indeed move several times; however, the evidence is not sufficient to outweigh the credibility issues raised at the hearing.

After examining all of the evidence, the panel concludes that the refugee protection claimants did not establish that they would face a serious possibility of persecution, or that, on a balance of probabilities, they would personally be subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to their lives, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if they were to return to Mexico.
For these reasons, the panel does not believe the claimants' allegations and concludes that they would not, on a balance of probabilities, be at risk of any harm should they return to Mexico.

For these reasons, the panel determines that the claimants are neither "Convention refugees" pursuant to section 96 of the IRPA, nor "persons in need of protection" within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

As a result, the panel rejects the refugee protection claims of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.
